catalog_quote: 2.1.4 Stress Harrington (33.0235) first noted that there are two main patterns of predictable word stress in Barbareño: stress that occurs on the penultimate syllable, and stress that occurs on the final syllable. Penultimate stress occurs generally when at least one of the final two syllables lacks a coda. (15) wó.qo 'hard tar; asphalt' ... (17) ʔé.neq 'woman' ... (19) yín.ċi 'to be hot' ... (21) ʔax.ta.wa.yán.pi 'shade' Final stress occurs when both of the final two syllables have a coda. (22) sul.kúw 'night' ... (26) waš.nax.yít 'tomorrow' Final stress also occurs when the word-final consonant has glottalization, regardless of the weight of the final two syllables, (27) siq.ċíʔ 'rainclouds' ... (32) ʔa.ṗi.t̓íʔ 'ladder' or when the onset of the final syllable has aspiration. (33) ta.kʰúy 'to carry' ... (37) mu.hú 'owl sp.' ... [Applegate 2017:25] The accent on Shmuwich words generally…

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding Wash 2001:33 passage and the Applegate 2017:25-26 secondary passage are both verbatim in copies we hold at the stated locators. (2) Deciding source: a 2001 UCSB dissertation phonology section built on Harrington's notes, backed by the 2017 interim reference grammar (Glottolog's only 'grammar' entry) - together the best available descriptions for a language with no speakers since 1965; no instrumental or JIPA study exists. (3) New evidence downloaded: Wash 1995:71-73 states the same rule in explicitly quantity-sensitive terms (coda = mora; final stress iff both syllables of the final foot are heavy, plus final glottalized coda or h-onset; otherwise penult; residue 'rare' and lexical) and quotes Harrington 33:0235 directly - this refines and confirms the 'weight' classification (what counts as heavy: CVC, right edge) and shows the 'generally' hedge in Wash 2001 covers only a small le

sources.quote: p.71: 'Stress assignment is determined by the weight of the two syllables in the word-final foot. Light syllables are monomoraic (with no coda); heavy syllables have a moraic coda. If either syllable is light, then main stress falls on the penultimate syllable, as seen in počóyi and ʔaqšwálaw below. If both syllables are heavy, then stress falls on the final syllable, as in wašnaxyít. Harrington (33:0235) was the first to note the existence of ultimate and penultimate stress in Barbareño.' Heavy-penult+light-final (súlku, kálpu, kálni) 'notably rare ... except in loanwords' -> penult. pp.72-73

sources.note: Fullest explicit moraic statement of the Barbareño stress rule (pp.68-73), with derivations and the 'rare, lexically marked' exceptions; strengthens the weight-sensitive reading behind our quantity-sensitive coding. downloaded now.
